CABLE THEFT

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cable theft goes beyond the piece of shiny metal – it’s a sophisticated criminal operation raking millions of rands for highly organized syndicated, crippling critical infrastructure.

Unique Selling Point:
- A GOOD NEWS CRIME STORY
- A SYSTEM THAT's WORKING TO KEEP CROOKS BEHIND BARS
- VISUALLY INTERESTING - CSI TYPE ELEMENTS, FOOTAGE OF PROJECTS & CATCHING CRIMINALS

Summary:
able theft is big business – run be criminal syndicates that feed an international export market worth hundreds of millions. The impact goes far beyond the value of the theft – it cripples essential infrastructure affecting South Africans and the economy.

Government has taken a stand and amended the Criminal Matters Act to ensure stricter bail conditions and harsher sentences that match the crime – and, it’s working!

We investigate this crime trend from the perspective of the investigators and prosecutors who are catching these criminals and putting them behind bars with hefty sentences.


Further information:
WHY DO WE CARE ABOUT CABLE THEFT? THE IMPACT IS SEVERE
It is just a piece of cable or a battery from a cellphone tower. It is trains that don’t operate, it is telecommunication systems that crash, it is power stations that can’t deliver power – the impact is real – it goes far and wide and affects South Africans across the board.

Expert – Leon van den Berg, quantifies the impact of cable theft looking at the value of the disruptions, the indirect resultant damage and what it means to society.

RECENT INSTANCE OF CABLE THEFT & THE CONSEQUENCES
In January two passenger trains collided in Pretoria – 620 people injured, 3 people killed.
Although the accident was not as a direct result of cable theft – it was as a result of cable theft – because the cables had been stolen the trains were operated manually and not on the automated signally system which opens the door to human error and tradgedy.

CSI-TYPE TECH CATCHING CRIMINALS
Roy Robertson leads a multi-displinary team that is tackling cable theft head on:
- criminologists to link syndicates and gang members to different cases
- ballistics experts forensically analyze and link cut cables and bolt cutters to crime scenes, finger printing, foot and tyre print collection – fascinating visuals of how they analyze evidence using state of the art microscopes and expertise to pin criminals to crime scenes.
- cyber crime experts track down cable theft dealers by infiltrating their social media networks – one crook posted a on FB of himself with stacks of cash, he left the location on – which happened to be very same location where a big hit happened the night before. SAPS were alerted – they moved in and arrested him – he got 15 years behind bars.
- Advocates help prep cases and support prosecutors to ensure the harshest sentences are applied.

They do work across South Africa for Eskom, Transnet, Prasa and Telkom and are considered the leaders in this field of investigation. They make use of heat activated and motion detection cameras to catch criminals on scenes.

THERE IS FOOTAGE AVAILABLE OF OPERATIONS FILMED FROM CHOPPERS.

PRICE THEFT HYPOTHESIS
Crime is influenced by economic factors. If the price of copper goes up so too will the number of cable theft incidents simply because there is more money to be made.

These criminals are clever - they know the system, they know the market.

INFORMANT - HIDDEN IDENTITY
We do an interview with an informant currently working with syndicates to explain the crime trend from their perspective - how & why it works.

EXPORT MARKET
Every month roughly 250 containers of high grade copper is exported illegally. We know this because since August 2015 no permits have been issued for the legal export of high grade copper. The rogues are exporting tons and tons of copper using the incorrect tariff codes to crook the system.

250 containers @ 24000kg x R80/kg
= R480 million LEAVING THE COUNTRY ILLEGALLY EVERY MONTH!!!!

KILL THE MARKET – KILL THE CRIME
These investigators are taking their investigation to the next level – they realise there is no point in arresting the cable cutter or runner – they need to get to syndicate and ensure they are put behind bars with unquestionable evidence if they are going to make a difference to this crime trend.

They use all their resources and attempt to take every case full circle. Catching the small guys just won’t cut it.

THE LAW IF WORKING
The Criminal Matters Amendment Act 18 of 2015 (the Act) is now operational, it commenced on 1 June 2016 and the sentences are finally starting to materialise with hefty sentences being handed down in 2018.

One syndicate of 11 members got 1232 years in total. Another group got over 900, and a man for stealing R700 of cable is sitting behind bars for 5 years. The NPA is taking full advantage of the amended legislation to send criminals a clear message – essential infrastructure related crime will not be tolerated.
According to the Government Gazette, the Act amends the –
• Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977, so as to regulate bail in respect of essential infrastructure-related offences;
• Criminal Law Amendment Act 105 of 1997, so as to regulate the imposition of discretionary minimum sentences for essential infrastructure-related offences and create a new offence relating to essential infrastructure; and
• Prevention of Organised Crime Act 121 of 1998, so as to insert a new offence in sch 1 to the Act and to provide for matters connected therewith.
The Act ensures that there are stricter conditions for the granting of bail in respect of essential infrastructure-related offences, there is also imposition of harsher sentences to perpetrators. The Act is viewed by most as a timely tool to deal with increasing acts of vandalism and theft of infrastructure.
Speaking on offences relating to essential infrastructure, s 3 of the Act states:
‘(1) Any person who unlawfully and intentionally –
(a) tampers with, damages or destroys essential infrastructure; or
(b) colludes with or assists another person in the commission, performance or carrying out of an activity referred to in paragraph (a),
and who knows or ought reasonably to have known or suspected that it is essential infrastructure, is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a period of imprisonment not exceeding 30 years or, in the case of a corporate body as contemplated in section 332(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977, a fine not exceeding R100 million.’

- COMBINED PRIVATE INVESTIGATIONS – ROY ROBERTSON
- CRIMINOLOGIST
- IMPACT ASSESSMENT EXPERT – LEON VAN DEN BERG
- NATIONAL PROSECUTION AUTHORITY
- INFORMANT

Press Release:


The Fightback Against Cable Theft
Frustrated with random power outages? Stranded, without phone connections or transport? Finally, crack investigators have real tools to fight back and bring cable theft criminals to book. The crime trend of cable theft borders on sabotage, as it targets copper cables from essential infrastructure such as power lines and communication networks. Highly organised syndicates rake in millions of Rands in this illicit trade. Carte Blanche meets law enforcers who are now able to take back the turf effectively, as new legislation ensures punishment that fits the crime, with sentences exceeding those for murder, for those caught stealing or selling stolen copper cables.
Producer: Nicky Troll
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: When your cellphone network goes down, it may not be your service provider’s fault. When you’re plunged into darkness and stuck in traffic, because the traffic light don’t work - Eskom might also not be to blame.

LINK: It’s a criminal network taking anything and everything they can carry from power cables, to copper to even batteries that run traffic lights and mobile networks towers – stealing from society and crippling the economy bit by bit. OPENING

STEPH: Every single day, as you and I sit here it is happening – there is no piece of infrastructure or place that is immune to this. //INT2 M4

VO: Criminals target essential infrastructure, costing the country in excess of 5 billion Rand every year – but that’s not counting the consequential losses – people can die.

22 miners are presumed dead at Optimum Coal Mine after cable thieves caused a gas explosion earlier this month.

In January, 620 people were injured, 3 were killed when two passenger trains collided in Pretoria – the root cause – also cable theft.

MOVE DR SITHOLE: // we are experiencing lawlessness at a rate that we have never seen before. INT1 M6

VO: The knock on effect of essential infrastructure crime is severe. Cable Theft damage has cost PRASA R625 million in just the last 10 months according to Group Chief Strategy Officer, Dr Sipho Sithole.

CUT DR SITHOLE: it is a massive challenge we are facing – not just as PRASA, but as a country //INT1 M10 // //talk to Eskom they will tell you the same thing, talk to Telkom they will tell you the same there the thing //INT1 M21

VO: This former cable thief turned informant says the rewards outweigh the risks, there’s quick cash to be made.

INFORMANT: it’s very, very dangerous, you can get caught, you can be injured, you can die, but we will do this because we are trying to live. INT1 M10
CLAIRE: Do you realise the impact?
INFORMANT: Ja, I know,
CLAIRE: BUT?
INFORMANT: Just because no money, no food, you must go. INT1 M13 /These people will never stop INT1 M16

VO: Cable theft is a part of life for the culprits, explains Criminologist Steph Jordaan.

STEPH: It’s become such a South African Trade mark to steal copper. The intergenerational element can’t be disputed because for years before and for years to come this is how my family put food on the table. INT2 M2

VO: These criminals are so brazen, they steal in broad daylight. Watch as these men cut out cables with a hacksaw at substation in Ekhuruleni in Gauteng – the result? A black out in the surrounding neighbourhood.

The rail system is targeted every day. In the Western Cape, Gangsters have monopolised cable theft – wrecking infrastructure as they go in with weapons to secure their loot and protect their turf.

Herman van den Berg is part of a specialist national private security outfit that tackles infrastructure crime. He heads up a ground team in the Cape - going toe to toe with gangsters.

HERMAN: // It is dangerous in here, // they shot at us a few times, // you must // show them your strength, if you show weakness, they will run over you. // INT1 M9

VO: PRASA’s central Cape Town line runs through the hub of ganglands. This video shows how thieves have gone as far as to dig up concrete to get to cables. The theft is so rampant that some sections of the line no longer run.

DR SITHOLE: We have got the Central Line that has been overtaken by thugs, //we’ve discovered about 40 km of cables having been dug out by people who come there armed. // INT1 M12

HERMAN: //all the gangsters have guns, they come with a gun, a knife and then a spade or a hacksaw to steal the cable.// INT2 M1

VO: Once they have the cable – the next step is to reprocess the material making the material unrecognisable. It’s done brazenly, out in plain sight.

We came across a scene in Khayelitsha close to the airport.

UPSOUNDS??????

But gangsters no longer have the upper hand – Van den Berg and his team are starting to take back the turf.

LINK: When it comes to essential infrastructure related crime – it’s not simply a case of theft or damage to property, it lends itself to sabotage and authorities are adamant that the punishment for the culprits must meet the crime… NPA

ADV JOHNSON: // this penalty is even more than murder INT1 M6

VO: Advocate Andrea Johnson of the National Prosecuting Authority, says the Criminal Matters Amendment Act, adopted in 2016, has been the ultimate game changer

ADV JOHNSON: // one is able to then better identify the crime and better deal with the crime, better deal with perpetrators INT1 M6

VO: Since 2016, if successfully prosecuted criminals found guilty of tampering, damaging or stealing essential infrastructure can get as much as 30 years direct imprisonment or a fine of up to R100 million.

Collaborative investigations run by private security, police and prosecutors are tapping into networks of informants, cyber crime analysis, suspect profiling and even incorporate forensic analysis to link criminals to cases.

DAVE: What we are bringing to the table is the physical evidence that the courts want to see // INT5 M2

VO: Using state of the art microscopes, investigators are able to link recovered materials and suspects to crime scenes explains Forensic Specialist Dave Pieterse.

DAVE: // this comes from the crime scene, this is the casing and there you can see – there is unique marks that was transferred on to the casing during the installation process, so that is a cut that is unique, there is another cut going over there, //
CLAIRE: perfect match
DAVE: // perfect fit physical match. INT3 M2

VO: They are even able to able link the tools recovered in suspects’ possession to crime scenes. Each and every bolt cutter will leave unique indentations and striation marks on the material.

DAVE: //it is just a matter of lining everything up with the dividing line in the middle – now you will see it matches from here all the way up and now I can conclude that the bolt cutter I used to cut the test with is also the bolt cutter that is responsible for cutting the cable on the crime scene. INT5 M1

VO: In 11 months, Van den Berg’s team of just 13 guys, have reduced the number of incidents by 70% in the Western Cape – nationally they arrest on average 85 infrastructure thieves every month with a conviction rate of 90%.

But as Van den Berg & team close in on illegal activity, gangs adapt their modus operandi to hide stolen material.

HERMAN: In the past they go to the bucket shop and the scrap dealer – now they take it to the small little house // HOKKIE INT 1 M3 They are receiving the cables, they are skinning the cables and then are they transporting by a vehicle to the scrap yards. HOKKIE INT 1 M2

VO: Van den Berg and his team caught 4 men in the act of skinning more than 845kg of cable destined for scrapyards – the street value is around R42000.

But criminals don’t just target cabling, they even steal deep cycle batteries used in mobile network towers. Watch as these thieves use grinders to cut out these batteries weighing over 50kg each. These batteries power the networks, keeping the country connected.

It’s a sought after commodity on the black market – both locally and in neighbouring countries.

HERMAN: // if you have a solar panel they use the battery for that to charge their phone and the lights in their house for free – so you have forever power in your house with this battery and a solar // CELL INT 1

VO: We accompanied Van den Berg on a joint operation to visit scrapyards in the area around the tracks. One of the dealers claimed he never buys cabling and that the thieves know it.

SCRAP GUY: These guys they come here they will just pass here
CLAIRE: but do they try to sell to you
SCRAP GUY: These guys don’t come to me, they are scared of me, mos, they call me impi – because I work with the neighbourhood watch. You can check my book, you never find copper. RAID INT1 M1

VO: Illegal cable is often hidden beneath the legitimate plastic and glass materials. The team searched the premises, but only found cable casings just meters from the yard.

CLAIRE: do you suspect that he could have some illegal copper
HERMAN: for sure – here’s the evidence – next to the railway line, a scrap dealer with a lot of // casings laying in front of his yard, it must be… SCRAP INT2 M1
CLAIRE: So how much value would this be all together?
HERMAN: // you’re talking about R600 – R700 for this little bit of cable standing here – and that is the scrap dealer market price // SCRAP INT5 M1

VO: Using the price-theft hypothesis, Jordaan explains that the price of metals and theft trends are linked.

STEPH: As the price of copper goes, up the theft of copper goes // CUT syndicate members are smart enough to have a look at the global export market and say we should rather sell our material next month or we should get rid of everything now – this shows you this is intelligent people, not your average thief. INT1 M16

LINK: The stolen material very rarely stays in the country, it changes hands until it eventually leaves South Africa illegally - destined for an international market.

VO: In the last three years, no permits have been issued for the legal export of high grade copper, syndicates use incorrect tariff codes to make the exports appear legitimate.

It’s estimated that roughly 250 containers of copper is allegedly exported to China and India – illegally - every month. At R80 per kilogram that’s in the region of R440 million leaving the country – illegally - every month. [250 containers @ 24000kg x R80/kg = R440 million]

The key to curbing this crime trend is to address the issue at grassroots level – eliminating the market to kill the crime. It starts building trust with community informants and delivering results says Van den Berg.

HERMAN: // you must show them progress, if there is arrests made you must go back to community tell them about it, provide them with feedback on the progress, that there is a sentence. INT1 M8

VO: And the sentences are jaw-dropping

 Five accused got a combined sentence of 451 years imprisonment [10 December 2018 ]
 While another syndicate of 11 members got a combined sentence of 1213 years [15 December 2017]

The NPA mean business - legislation even provides for hefty sentences for simply tampering with infrastructure explains Advocate Johnson.

ADV JOHNSON: They had dug open a trench, with the view to steal the cable, they had yet to steal the cable, // had they stolen the cable those would have been the implications – they were sentenced to 15 years imprisonment direct INT1 M8

STEPH: what the suspects don’t understand even if you steal 10cm the impact is exactly the same as if you would have stolen 100m. INT1 M13

ADV JOHNSON: // when we do not have our basic services running on any given day – the country looses millions regardless of which sector it is in//INT1 M4// what is stolen is not necessarily what is retrieved and or recovered. // INT1 M7 FROM THE BEGINNING //

VO: The impact is far greater than simply the value of the piece of cable that is stolen - combatting this crime trend is not an option – it is a priority.











 



PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Essential infrastructure crime beyond cable theft – it’s a sophisticated criminal operation crippling the country and raking millions of rands in illicit trade for syndicates.

PROMO 2
VO: It borders on sabotage - essential infrastructure crime impacts on basic services delivery & devastates the country. But new legislation introduces punishment that finally fits the crime.


PROMO 3
VO: Essential infrastructure crime equates to sabotage. Stealing a piece of copper cable could land you behind bars for a very long time!

ADV JOHNSON: // this penalty is even more than murder INT1 M6

Carte Blanche meets law enforcers who are now able to take back the turf effectively, as new legislation ensures punishment that fits the crime, with sentences exceeding those for murder, for those caught stealing or selling stolen copper cables. Producer: Nicky Troll Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: STRUCTURE VO: When your cellphone network goes down, it may not be your service provider’s fault. When you’re plunged into darkness and stuck in traffic, because the traffic light don’t work - Eskom might also not be to blame. LINK: It’s a criminal network taking anything and everything they can carry from power cables, to copper to even batteries that run traffic lights and mobile networks towers – stealing from society and crippling the economy bit by bit. OPENING STEPH: Every single day, as you and I sit here it is happening – there is no piece of infrastructure or place that is immune to this. //INT2 M4 VO: Criminals target essential infrastructure, costing the country in excess of 5 billion Rand every year – but that’s not counting the consequential losses – people can die. 22 miners are presumed dead at Optimum Coal Mine after cable thieves caused a gas explosion earlier this month. In January, 620 people were injured, 3 were killed when two passenger trains collided in Pretoria – the root cause – also cable theft. MOVE DR SITHOLE: // we are experiencing lawlessness at a rate that we have never seen before. INT1 M6 VO: The knock on effect of essential infrastructure crime is severe. Cable Theft damage has cost PRASA R625 million in just the last 10 months according to Group Chief Strategy Officer, Dr Sipho Sithole. CUT DR SITHOLE: it is a massive challenge we are facing – not just as PRASA, but as a country //INT1 M10 // //talk to Eskom they will tell you the same thing, talk to Telkom they will tell you the same there the thing //INT1 M21 VO: This former cable thief turned informant says the rewards outweigh the risks, there’s quick cash to be made. INFORMANT: it’s very, very dangerous, you can get caught, you can be injured, you can die, but we will do this because we are trying to live. INT1 M10 CLAIRE: Do you realise the impact? INFORMANT: Ja, I know, CLAIRE: BUT? INFORMANT: Just because no money, no food, you must go. INT1 M13 /These people will never stop INT1 M16 VO: Cable theft is a part of life for the culprits, explains Criminologist Steph Jordaan. STEPH: It’s become such a South African Trade mark to steal copper. The intergenerational element can’t be disputed because for years before and for years to come this is how my family put food on the table. INT2 M2 VO: These criminals are so brazen, they steal in broad daylight. Watch as these men cut out cables with a hacksaw at substation in Ekhuruleni in Gauteng – the result? A black out in the surrounding neighbourhood. The rail system is targeted every day. In the Western Cape, Gangsters have monopolised cable theft – wrecking infrastructure as they go in with weapons to secure their loot and protect their turf. Herman van den Berg is part of a specialist national private security outfit that tackles infrastructure crime. He heads up a ground team in the Cape - going toe to toe with gangsters. HERMAN: // It is dangerous in here, // they shot at us a few times, // you must // show them your strength, if you show weakness, they will run over you. // INT1 M9 VO: PRASA’s central Cape Town line runs through the hub of ganglands. This video shows how thieves have gone as far as to dig up concrete to get to cables. The theft is so rampant that some sections of the line no longer run. DR SITHOLE: We have got the Central Line that has been overtaken by thugs, //we’ve discovered about 40 km of cables having been dug out by people who come there armed. // INT1 M12 HERMAN: //all the gangsters have guns, they come with a gun, a knife and then a spade or a hacksaw to steal the cable.// INT2 M1 VO: Once they have the cable – the next step is to reprocess the material making the material unrecognisable. It’s done brazenly, out in plain sight. We came across a scene in Khayelitsha close to the airport. UPSOUNDS?????? But gangsters no longer have the upper hand – Van den Berg and his team are starting to take back the turf. LINK: When it comes to essential infrastructure related crime – it’s not simply a case of theft or damage to property, it lends itself to sabotage and authorities are adamant that the punishment for the culprits must meet the crime… NPA ADV JOHNSON: // this penalty is even more than murder INT1 M6 VO: Advocate Andrea Johnson of the National Prosecuting Authority, says the Criminal Matters Amendment Act, adopted in 2016, has been the ultimate game changer ADV JOHNSON: // one is able to then better identify the crime and better deal with the crime, better deal with perpetrators INT1 M6 VO: Since 2016, if successfully prosecuted criminals found guilty of tampering, damaging or stealing essential infrastructure can get as much as 30 years direct imprisonment or a fine of up to R100 million. Collaborative investigations run by private security, police and prosecutors are tapping into networks of informants, cyber crime analysis, suspect profiling and even incorporate forensic analysis to link criminals to cases. DAVE: What we are bringing to the table is the physical evidence that the courts want to see // INT5 M2 VO: Using state of the art microscopes, investigators are able to link recovered materials and suspects to crime scenes explains Forensic Specialist Dave Pieterse. DAVE: // this comes from the crime scene, this is the casing and there you can see – there is unique marks that was transferred on to the casing during the installation process, so that is a cut that is unique, there is another cut going over there, // CLAIRE: perfect match DAVE: // perfect fit physical match. INT3 M2 VO: They are even able to able link the tools recovered in suspects’ possession to crime scenes. Each and every bolt cutter will leave unique indentations and striation marks on the material. DAVE: //it is just a matter of lining everything up with the dividing line in the middle – now you will see it matches from here all the way up and now I can conclude that the bolt cutter I used to cut the test with is also the bolt cutter that is responsible for cutting the cable on the crime scene. INT5 M1 VO: In 11 months, Van den Berg’s team of just 13 guys, have reduced the number of incidents by 70% in the Western Cape – nationally they arrest on average 85 infrastructure thieves every month with a conviction rate of 90%. But as Van den Berg & team close in on illegal activity, gangs adapt their modus operandi to hide stolen material. HERMAN: In the past they go to the bucket shop and the scrap dealer – now they take it to the small little house // HOKKIE INT 1 M3 They are receiving the cables, they are skinning the cables and then are they transporting by a vehicle to the scrap yards. HOKKIE INT 1 M2 VO: Van den Berg and his team caught 4 men in the act of skinning more than 845kg of cable destined for scrapyards – the street value is around R42000. But criminals don’t just target cabling, they even steal deep cycle batteries used in mobile network towers. Watch as these thieves use grinders to cut out these batteries weighing over 50kg each. These batteries power the networks, keeping the country connected. It’s a sought after commodity on the black market – both locally and in neighbouring countries. HERMAN: // if you have a solar panel they use the battery for that to charge their phone and the lights in their house for free – so you have forever power in your house with this battery and a solar // CELL INT 1 VO: We accompanied Van den Berg on a joint operation to visit scrapyards in the area around the tracks. One of the dealers claimed he never buys cabling and that the thieves know it. SCRAP GUY: These guys they come here they will just pass here CLAIRE: but do they try to sell to you SCRAP GUY: These guys don’t come to me, they are scared of me, mos, they call me impi – because I work with the neighbourhood watch. You can check my book, you never find copper. RAID INT1 M1 VO: Illegal cable is often hidden beneath the legitimate plastic and glass materials. The team searched the premises, but only found cable casings just meters from the yard. CLAIRE: do you suspect that he could have some illegal copper HERMAN: for sure – here’s the evidence – next to the railway line, a scrap dealer with a lot of // casings laying in front of his yard, it must be… SCRAP INT2 M1 CLAIRE: So how much value would this be all together? HERMAN: // you’re talking about R600 – R700 for this little bit of cable standing here – and that is the scrap dealer market price // SCRAP INT5 M1 VO: Using the price-theft hypothesis, Jordaan explains that the price of metals and theft trends are linked. STEPH: As the price of copper goes, up the theft of copper goes // CUT syndicate members are smart enough to have a look at the global export market and say we should rather sell our material next month or we should get rid of everything now – this shows you this is intelligent people, not your average thief. INT1 M16 LINK: The stolen material very rarely stays in the country, it changes hands until it eventually leaves South Africa illegally - destined for an international market. VO: In the last three years, no permits have been issued for the legal export of high grade copper, syndicates use incorrect tariff codes to make the exports appear legitimate. It’s estimated that roughly 250 containers of copper is allegedly exported to China and India – illegally - every month. At R80 per kilogram that’s in the region of R440 million leaving the country – illegally - every month. [250 containers @ 24000kg x R80/kg = R440 million] The key to curbing this crime trend is to address the issue at grassroots level – eliminating the market to kill the crime. It starts building trust with community informants and delivering results says Van den Berg. HERMAN: // you must show them progress, if there is arrests made you must go back to community tell them about it, provide them with feedback on the progress, that there is a sentence. INT1 M8 VO: And the sentences are jaw-dropping  Five accused got a combined sentence of 451 years imprisonment [10 December 2018 ]  While another syndicate of 11 members got a combined sentence of 1213 years [15 December 2017] The NPA mean business - legislation even provides for hefty sentences for simply tampering with infrastructure explains Advocate Johnson. ADV JOHNSON: They had dug open a trench, with the view to steal the cable, they had yet to steal the cable, // had they stolen the cable those would have been the implications – they were sentenced to 15 years imprisonment direct INT1 M8 STEPH: what the suspects don’t understand even if you steal 10cm the impact is exactly the same as if you would have stolen 100m. INT1 M13 ADV JOHNSON: // when we do not have our basic services running on any given day – the country looses millions regardless of which sector it is in//INT1 M4// what is stolen is not necessarily what is retrieved and or recovered. // INT1 M7 FROM THE BEGINNING // VO: The impact is far greater than simply the value of the piece of cable that is stolen - combatting this crime trend is not an option – it is a priority. PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: Essential infrastructure crime beyond cable theft – it’s a sophisticated criminal operation crippling the country and raking millions of rands in illicit trade for syndicates. PROMO 2 VO: It borders on sabotage - essential infrastructure crime impacts on basic services delivery & devastates the country. But new legislation introduces punishment that finally fits the crime. PROMO 3 VO: Essential infrastructure crime equates to sabotage. Stealing a piece of copper cable could land you behind bars for a very long time! ADV JOHNSON: // this penalty is even more than murder INT1 M6 Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for CABLE THEFT (5382) Nicky Troll 03 March 2019

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Cable theft goes beyond the piece of shiny metal – it’s a sophisticated criminal operation raking millions of rands for highly organized syndicated, crippling critical infrastructure.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: - A GOOD NEWS CRIME STORY - A SYSTEM THAT's WORKING TO KEEP CROOKS BEHIND BARS - VISUALLY INTERESTING - CSI TYPE ELEMENTS, FOOTAGE OF PROJECTS & CATCHING CRIMINALS
metadata.Summary: able theft is big business – run be criminal syndicates that feed an international export market worth hundreds of millions. The impact goes far beyond the value of the theft – it cripples essential infrastructure affecting South Africans and the economy. Government has taken a stand and amended the Criminal Matters Act to ensure stricter bail conditions and harsher sentences that match the crime – and, it’s working! We investigate this crime trend from the perspective of the investigators and prosecutors who are catching these criminals and putting them behind bars with hefty sentences.
metadata.Further information: WHY DO WE CARE ABOUT CABLE THEFT? THE IMPACT IS SEVERE It is just a piece of cable or a battery from a cellphone tower. It is trains that don’t operate, it is telecommunication systems that crash, it is power stations that can’t deliver power – the impact is real – it goes far and wide and affects South Africans across the board. Expert – Leon van den Berg, quantifies the impact of cable theft looking at the value of the disruptions, the indirect resultant damage and what it means to society. RECENT INSTANCE OF CABLE THEFT & THE CONSEQUENCES In January two passenger trains collided in Pretoria – 620 people injured, 3 people killed. Although the accident was not as a direct result of cable theft – it was as a result of cable theft – because the cables had been stolen the trains were operated manually and not on the automated signally system which opens the door to human error and tradgedy. CSI-TYPE TECH CATCHING CRIMINALS Roy Robertson leads a multi-displinary team that is tackling cable theft head on: - criminologists to link syndicates and gang members to different cases - ballistics experts forensically analyze and link cut cables and bolt cutters to crime scenes, finger printing, foot and tyre print collection – fascinating visuals of how they analyze evidence using state of the art microscopes and expertise to pin criminals to crime scenes. - cyber crime experts track down cable theft dealers by infiltrating their social media networks – one crook posted a on FB of himself with stacks of cash, he left the location on – which happened to be very same location where a big hit happened the night before. SAPS were alerted – they moved in and arrested him – he got 15 years behind bars. - Advocates help prep cases and support prosecutors to ensure the harshest sentences are applied. They do work across South Africa for Eskom, Transnet, Prasa and Telkom and are considered the leaders in this field of investigation. They make use of heat activated and motion detection cameras to catch criminals on scenes. THERE IS FOOTAGE AVAILABLE OF OPERATIONS FILMED FROM CHOPPERS. PRICE THEFT HYPOTHESIS Crime is influenced by economic factors. If the price of copper goes up so too will the number of cable theft incidents simply because there is more money to be made. These criminals are clever - they know the system, they know the market. INFORMANT - HIDDEN IDENTITY We do an interview with an informant currently working with syndicates to explain the crime trend from their perspective - how & why it works. EXPORT MARKET Every month roughly 250 containers of high grade copper is exported illegally. We know this because since August 2015 no permits have been issued for the legal export of high grade copper. The rogues are exporting tons and tons of copper using the incorrect tariff codes to crook the system. 250 containers @ 24000kg x R80/kg = R480 million LEAVING THE COUNTRY ILLEGALLY EVERY MONTH!!!! KILL THE MARKET – KILL THE CRIME These investigators are taking their investigation to the next level – they realise there is no point in arresting the cable cutter or runner – they need to get to syndicate and ensure they are put behind bars with unquestionable evidence if they are going to make a difference to this crime trend. They use all their resources and attempt to take every case full circle. Catching the small guys just won’t cut it. THE LAW IF WORKING The Criminal Matters Amendment Act 18 of 2015 (the Act) is now operational, it commenced on 1 June 2016 and the sentences are finally starting to materialise with hefty sentences being handed down in 2018. One syndicate of 11 members got 1232 years in total. Another group got over 900, and a man for stealing R700 of cable is sitting behind bars for 5 years. The NPA is taking full advantage of the amended legislation to send criminals a clear message – essential infrastructure related crime will not be tolerated. According to the Government Gazette, the Act amends the – • Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977, so as to regulate bail in respect of essential infrastructure-related offences; • Criminal Law Amendment Act 105 of 1997, so as to regulate the imposition of discretionary minimum sentences for essential infrastructure-related offences and create a new offence relating to essential infrastructure; and • Prevention of Organised Crime Act 121 of 1998, so as to insert a new offence in sch 1 to the Act and to provide for matters connected therewith. The Act ensures that there are stricter conditions for the granting of bail in respect of essential infrastructure-related offences, there is also imposition of harsher sentences to perpetrators. The Act is viewed by most as a timely tool to deal with increasing acts of vandalism and theft of infrastructure. Speaking on offences relating to essential infrastructure, s 3 of the Act states: ‘(1) Any person who unlawfully and intentionally – (a) tampers with, damages or destroys essential infrastructure; or (b) colludes with or assists another person in the commission, performance or carrying out of an activity referred to in paragraph (a), and who knows or ought reasonably to have known or suspected that it is essential infrastructure, is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a period of imprisonment not exceeding 30 years or, in the case of a corporate body as contemplated in section 332(2) of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1977, a fine not exceeding R100 million.’ INTERVIEWS - PRASA - COMBINED PRIVATE INVESTIGATIONS – ROY ROBERTSON - CRIMINOLOGIST - IMPACT ASSESSMENT EXPERT – LEON VAN DEN BERG - NATIONAL PROSECUTION AUTHORITY - INFORMANT
